div.head: Hn 77.2a
div.ab: Aliquando autem erit sicut dominus eius uoluerit: ‘uitulus autem matris est, cuiuscunque taurus alluserit’.
div.note: New row (October 2026): Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 594 (two independent readings of the page images, differences settled against the page)

note.seg: den Stand des Kindes entscheidet der der Mutter in der Frage der Ehelichkeit, nach einem anderen, dasselbe Bild benutzenden Sprichwort; King John (Scene I) bei Shakespeare sagt, der Ehemann der von Richard I. geschwängerten Frau might have kept This calf bred from his cow from all the world; Somner citirt für England 17. Jhs.: Whosoever [He that Howell Lex. Tetraglotton. 1659] bulls the cow, the good man [Ehemann] must keep the calf

the child’s status is determined by the mother’s in the question of legitimacy, according to another proverb that uses the same image; King John (Scene I) in Shakespeare says that the husband of the woman made pregnant by Richard I might have kept This calf bred from his cow from all the world; Somner cites for 17th-cent. England: Whosoever [He that Howell Lex. Tetraglotton. 1659] bulls the cow, the good man [husband] must keep the calf
matris est cuiuscunque fügt [aus folgender Zeile] hinzu Sl Tw
matris est cuiuscunque added [from the following line] by Sl Tw

Offenbar verstand ein mächtiger Dynast, den Status (s. u. 78, 2b) nach Belieben festzusetzen, wenn des Betreffenden Vater oder Mutter unfrei war. Dass es sich um Uneheliche handelt, wie Kemble Saxons I 207 meint, nehmen Graf und Dietherr Dt. Rechtssprichw. 61 und Pol Mai I 405f. nicht an.—Aber auch dass allgemein das Kind der ärgeren Hand folge, lese ich nicht mit Pol Mai aus Hn heraus. Glanvilla oder gar späteres MA. (ebd.) darf man nicht mit Allen (bei Thorpe Anc. laws 273) zur Erklärung heranziehen

Evidently a powerful magnate knew how to fix the status (see below 78, 2b) at will when the father or mother of the person concerned was unfree. That illegitimate children are meant, as Kemble Saxons I 207 thinks, is not accepted by Graf and Dietherr Dt. Rechtssprichw. 61 or by Pol Mai I 405f.—But neither do I read out of Hn, with Pol Mai, that in general the child follows the worse hand. One may not, with Allen (in Thorpe Anc. laws 273), draw on Glanvilla, or even the later Middle Ages (ibid.), to explain it
